questions.q: In hydra, repeated cell division at one spot on the parent's body produces a small outgrowth that later separates and lives on its own. What is this outgrowth called?
questions.a: a bud: the process is budding, an asexual method seen in hydra and yeast.

questions.q: Black patches of mould appear on one damp wall of a house, and a few weeks later on other damp walls too. Which reason fits the chapter best?
o: The mould forms millions of lightweight spores that float on air currents
The mould's hyphae grow through the bricks from one wall to the next
The mould forms buds that roll along the floor to other walls
The mould needs two parents, so it appears wherever two colonies meet
questions.a: The mould forms millions of lightweight spores that float on air currents and germinate where they find moisture.

questions.q: A nursery grows 50 money plants from stem pieces of one mother plant. A customer asks why all 50 have exactly the same leaf pattern as the mother. Which reply is correct?
o: They came from one parent's stem, so they are genetically identical
They were all pollinated by the same insect, so they look alike
They were formed by meiosis, so each carries half of the mother's chromosomes
They were formed from spores that the mother plant released into the soil
questions.a: They came from one parent's stem, so they are genetically identical: vegetative propagation involves only one parent.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about fungi.
I. Rhizopus forms its spores inside a sac-like structure.
II. Antibiotics such as penicillin and amoxicillin are derived from fungi.
III. Mould spores are usually many-celled and heavy, so they settle close to the parent colony.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is wrong: spores are lightweight, usually single-celled, and float easily through air currents.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Asexual reproduction helps an organism increase its population quickly when conditions are favourable.
Reason (R): In asexual reproduction, the offspring are produced by meiosis.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: asexual reproduction is fast, but the process behind it is mitosis, not meiosis.

questions.q: True or False? Budding is a method of reproduction seen only in plants. Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Budding is seen in yeast, a unicellular fungus, and in hydra, a multicellular animal.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: budding occurs in yeast and in hydra (an animal), not only in plants

questions.q: Name the method of vegetative propagation in each case. (a) The middle part of a thin, flexible lemon twig is buried in soil while still attached to the plant; after roots form, it is cut away. (b) A piece of a shoot, with the leaves removed from its lower half, is pushed about halfway into soil mixed with compost.
questions.a: (a) Layering. (b) Cutting.
s: (a) Layering
(b) Cutting

questions.q: Kabir says, 'A Bryophyllum plantlet, a yeast bud and a Rhizopus spore are formed in three different ways, so the young ones will differ from their parents by three different amounts.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. The methods do differ: vegetative propagation from a leaf, budding, and spore formation. But all three rest on mitosis, which gives daughter cells with the same chromosomes as the parent, so all the young ones are genetically identical clones; they do not differ from their parents at all.
s: Names the three different methods: vegetative propagation, budding, spore formation
States that all three depend on mitosis, giving the same chromosomes as the parent
Verdict: partly right; the offspring are all clones, so the 'different amounts' part is wrong

questions.q:
A town council in Maharashtra has two waste problems: heaps of rotting vegetable-market waste, and wastewater from a metal-plating unit that carries heavy metals. A local college ran a trial on market waste. A 200 kg heap seeded with fungal spores and kept warm and moist shrank to 80 kg of compost in 30 days. An untreated 200 kg heap shrank only to 170 kg in the same time.
(a) By how many kilograms did each heap shrink, and how many times larger was the treated heap's loss?
(b) Using how fungi reproduce, explain why seeding the heap with spores and keeping it warm and moist made it break down so fast.
(c) Apart from degrading organic waste, name one other way in which fungi help society, as described in the chapter.
(d) This year the council can pay for fungal treatment of only one of the two problems. Give one reason in favour of each choice and state which you would pick.
questions.a: (a) Treated heap: 200 - 80 = 120 kg; untreated heap: 200 - 170 = 30 kg; 120 / 30 = 4 times larger. (b) Fungi grow very fast by forming spores; spores germinate quickly into new individuals when they find moisture and nutrients, and warmth helps them grow, so the heap was soon covered by fast-multiplying fungi that degraded it. (c) Fungi help remove heavy metals from industrial waste, or they are the source of antibiotics such as penicillin and amoxicillin. (d) Market waste: the trial shows a four-fold faster breakdown, so the benefit is proven. Plating wastewater: heavy metals are harmful and fungi help remove them, but this use has not been tested here. Either choice is accepted with a reason that uses the data or the chapter.
s: (a) 120 kg and 30 kg; 4 times larger
(b) Spores formed in huge numbers germinate quickly in warmth and moisture, so fungi multiply fast and degrade the waste
(c) Removing heavy metals from industrial waste, or antibiotics such as penicillin
(d) One reason for each option and a justified choice

questions.q: For each case, name the method of asexual reproduction taking place. (i) A ginger piece left in a kitchen basket sprouts new shoots. (ii) Under a microscope, a yeast cell in sugar solution shows a small round outgrowth. (iii) A damp roti kept in a warm dabba for three days is covered with fuzzy threads carrying round sacs. (iv) A small outgrowth on a hydra grows larger and then detaches to live on its own. (v) A banana farmer receives thousands of healthy plantlets grown in a laboratory from the shoot tips of a parent plant.
questions.a: (i) Vegetative propagation from a fleshy underground stem. (ii) Budding. (iii) Spore formation by a mould such as Rhizopus. (iv) Budding. (v) Tissue culture, a method of vegetative propagation.
s: (i) Vegetative propagation (underground stem)
(ii) Budding in yeast
(iii) Spore formation by mould
(iv) Budding in hydra
(v) Tissue culture

questions.q: What are the thread-like structures in the nucleus of a cell that carry genetic information called?
questions.a: chromosomes: each species has a fixed number of them in its cells.

questions.q: The body cells of a garden pea plant have 14 chromosomes. How many chromosomes will the egg cell inside one of its ovules carry?
questions.a: 7: the egg is a gamete formed by meiosis, which halves the chromosome number (14 / 2 = 7).

questions.q: A parent cell with 8 chromosomes (4 pairs) divides by meiosis. Which statement correctly describes the cells formed?
o: Each has 4 chromosomes, one from each pair, and is used only for reproduction
Each has 8 chromosomes, the same as the parent, and is used to repair the body
Each has 4 chromosomes and later grows into a new body cell of the parent
Each has 16 chromosomes, two from each pair, so that the zygote can have 8
questions.a: Each has 4 chromosomes, one from each pair, and is used only for reproduction: these haploid cells are gametes.

questions.q:
Match each term with its meaning.
1. Diploid
2. Haploid
3. Gamete
4. Clone
a. Half the chromosome number, one chromosome from each pair
b. Offspring genetically identical to its single parent
c. The full chromosome number of a body cell, in pairs
d. A haploid cell used only for reproduction
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-d, 4-b: diploid is the full paired number, haploid is half, a gamete is a haploid reproductive cell, and a clone is identical to its single parent.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Children of the same parents are genetically different from one another.
Reason (R): Gametes are haploid cells that are used only for reproduction.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the differences come from the random way chromosome pairs separate in meiosis, giving each gamete a different mix.

questions.q: Differentiate asexual reproduction from sexual reproduction on two points: (a) the number of parents involved, and (b) how alike the offspring are to their parents.
questions.a: (a) Asexual reproduction involves one parent; sexual reproduction involves two parents. (b) Asexual offspring are genetically identical to the parent (clones); sexual offspring receive a mix of characteristics from both parents, so they differ from them.
s: (a) One parent in asexual, two parents in sexual reproduction
(b) Asexual offspring are identical clones; sexual offspring carry a mix and show variation

questions.q: A student looks at two cells from the same dog. One cell has 78 chromosomes and the other has 39. (a) Which of the two is a gamete, and which is a body cell? (b) Name the cell division that formed the 39-chromosome cell, and say how many chromosomes the zygote will have if this cell fuses with a gamete of the opposite sex.
questions.a: (a) The 39-chromosome cell is a gamete; the 78-chromosome cell is a body cell. (b) Meiosis formed it; the zygote will have 39 + 39 = 78 chromosomes, the same as the parents.
s: (a) 39 = gamete, 78 = body cell
(b) Meiosis; zygote has 78 chromosomes

questions.q: Priya says, 'Every human sperm carries exactly 23 chromosomes, so all the sperm made by one man carry the same genetic information.' Check her claim.
questions.a: No. The number is right: each sperm has 23 chromosomes. But during meiosis the two chromosomes of each pair separate at random, and each gamete receives only one chromosome from each pair. With 23 pairs, a very large number of different combinations is possible, so different sperm of the same man carry different mixes of characters.
s: Agrees that each sperm has 23 chromosomes
Explains that one chromosome of each pair goes to a gamete at random during meiosis
Verdict: No; with 23 pairs the combinations are many, so sperm differ

questions.q: Explain (i) how variation arises among the offspring of sexual reproduction, (ii) one way in which variation helps some individuals, with an example from the chapter, and (iii) what variation does for a species over a very long time.
questions.a: (i) During meiosis chromosome pairs separate at random, so each gamete gets a different combination, and fusion of gametes from two parents gives each child a unique combination. (ii) Some individuals adapt better to changing environments, for example people who can tolerate low oxygen at high altitudes or digest milk as adults. (iii) Over time this contributes to evolution and helps the species survive.
s: (i) Random separation of chromosome pairs in meiosis gives unique combinations
(ii) Helps some adapt to changing environments, with a chapter example
(iii) Contributes to survival of the species and evolution over time

questions.q: A new leaf disease reaches a district. Field A has 1000 banana plants, all produced by tissue culture from one mother plant. Field B has 1000 plants of a crop grown from seeds formed after cross-pollination. Assume that whether a plant resists the disease depends only on its genetic information. (i) Say how the plants in each field were formed and whether they are genetically alike. (ii) Explain why the plants of field A are likely to be either all resistant or all affected. (iii) In field B, 120 plants resist the disease. What percentage is this? (iv) Which field is better placed to keep the crop going when a new disease appears, and why?
questions.a: (i) Field A: asexual reproduction by tissue culture, so all are genetically identical clones of the mother plant. Field B: sexual reproduction, so the plants show variation. (ii) Identical plants carry the same genetic information, so they respond to the disease in the same way. (iii) 120 / 1000 x 100 = 12%. (iv) Field B: variation means some plants (12% here) resist the disease and can continue the crop, while in field A a disease that affects one plant can affect all.
s: (i) Field A clones by tissue culture; field B varied, from sexual reproduction
(ii) Identical genetic information, so identical response to the disease
(iv) Field B, because variation leaves some resistant plants to carry the crop on

questions.q: In a flower bud, which part forms the green outermost whorl that covers all the other parts?
questions.a: sepal: it is the green covering around all the parts at the bud stage.

questions.q: Which part of a flower produces the pollen grains that contain male gametes?
questions.a: anther: it sits on the filament, and the two together form the stamen.

questions.q: Pollen from a flower of one rice plant reaches the stigma of a flower on a different rice plant in the same field. Which statement is correct?
o: This is cross-pollination, most likely carried by the wind
This is self-pollination, because both plants are rice
This is cross-pollination, carried by birds such as sunbirds
This is fertilisation, because the pollen has reached a stigma
questions.a: This is cross-pollination, most likely carried by the wind: the pollen moved between two plants of the same type, and rice is wind-pollinated.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about pollination strategies.
I. In Vallisneria, water currents carry pollen from one flower to another.
II. Insect-pollinated flowers usually have a long, feathery stigma to trap pollen.
III. Flowers of the coral tree are pollinated by birds.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: a long, feathery stigma belongs to wind-pollinated flowers; insect-pollinated flowers have a sticky stigma.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The stigma of a wheat flower is long and feathery.
Reason (R): Wheat is pollinated by wind, and a feathery stigma traps the light pollen grains carried by the wind.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the feathery stigma is an adaptation for trapping wind-borne pollen.

questions.q: True or False? Self-pollination can take place only within one single flower. Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Self-pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma of the same flower or of another flower on the same plant.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: pollen may also go to another flower of the same plant

questions.q: (a) Name the two parts of a stamen. (b) State what the anther produces.
questions.a: (a) Filament and anther. (b) The anther produces pollen grains, which contain the male gametes.
s: (a) Filament and anther
(b) Pollen grains containing male gametes

questions.q: A compatible pollen grain lands on the stigma of a mustard flower. Describe in order what happens (i) on the stigma and in the style, (ii) when the male gamete reaches the ovule, and (iii) to the product of that fusion.
questions.a: (i) The pollen grain produces a pollen tube that grows down through the style into the ovary. (ii) The male gamete moves through the tube to the ovule and fuses with the egg cell; this is fertilisation. (iii) The fertilised egg, the zygote, later develops into an embryo.
s: (i) Pollen tube grows down through the style into the ovary
(ii) Male gamete fuses with the egg cell in the ovule (fertilisation)
(iii) Zygote forms and develops into an embryo

questions.q:
A seed company in Punjab wants a high-yield wheat variety that also resists a leaf disease. It tries three ways. Way 1: farmers keep seed only from the healthiest plants each year; over 6 seasons, the share of diseased plants falls from 40% to 25%. Way 2: stamens are removed from flowers of the high-yield variety, the flowers are bagged, and pollen from a disease-resistant variety is dusted on by hand; the first crop shows 10% diseased plants. Way 3: the genetic material for resistance is inserted into the DNA of the high-yield variety in a laboratory; the first trial shows 5% diseased plants.
(a) Name the plant breeding method used in each way.
(b) In Way 2, why are the flowers bagged after the stamens are removed?
(c) By how many percentage points did Way 1 lower the share of diseased plants, and by how much per season on average?
(d) The company has no laboratory and wants a better variety within one season. Which way should it choose? Justify using the data.
questions.a: (a) Way 1: selective breeding. Way 2: artificial hybridisation. Way 3: genetic engineering. (b) To prevent self-pollination, so that only the chosen pollen reaches the stigma. (c) 40 - 25 = 15 percentage points, which is 15 / 6 = 2.5 points per season. (d) Way 2: it needs no laboratory, unlike Way 3, and it gave 10% diseased plants in its first crop, while Way 1 took 6 seasons to reach only 25%.
s: (a) Selective breeding, artificial hybridisation, genetic engineering
(b) Bagging prevents self-pollination
(c) 15 percentage points; 2.5 per season
(d) Way 2, with reasons from the data (no lab needed; 10% in one crop versus 25% after 6 seasons)

questions.q: A school garden grows four plants: wheat in a bed, Hydrilla in a small pond, sunflower in a bed, and a young coral tree in a large pot. (i) Name the pollinating agent of wheat and of Hydrilla. (ii) Name the pollinating agent of sunflower and of the coral tree. To stop pests, the gardener covers every plant with a fine net that keeps out all insects and birds but does not block air or water movement. (iii) Will the wheat still set seed? Explain. (iv) Will the Hydrilla still set seed? Explain. (v) Evaluate the effect of the net on the sunflower and the coral tree, and say what will happen to their fruits and seeds.
questions.a: (i) Wheat: wind. Hydrilla: water. (ii) Sunflower: insects such as bees and butterflies. Coral tree: birds such as sunbirds and the Indian white-eye. (iii) Yes: wind still carries the light pollen to the feathery stigmas. (iv) Yes: water currents still carry the pollen from flower to flower. (v) The net keeps out their pollinators, so pollen does not reach the stigma; without pollination there is no fertilisation, so no fruits or seeds form. The net protects against pests but costs these two plants their seeds.
s: (i) Wheat by wind, Hydrilla by water
(ii) Sunflower by insects, coral tree by birds
(iii) Wheat sets seed: wind pollination is not blocked
(iv) Hydrilla sets seed: water pollination is not blocked
(v) Sunflower and coral tree: no pollinators, so no pollination, no fertilisation, no fruit or seed

questions.q: In which group of animals does fertilisation take place inside the body of the female?
o: all animals that live in water
questions.a: reptiles, birds and mammals: this is internal fertilisation.

questions.q: A lizard egg kept in a warm box at a science centre hatches directly into a young lizard, with no larval stage. Which reason fits the chapter?
o: Each reptile egg holds enough yolk to nourish the embryo until it hatches
Lizards show external fertilisation, so their eggs develop much faster in warmth
The embryo feeds on organic waste that seeps into the egg through the shell
The young lizard is fed by its mother with breast milk while inside the egg
questions.a: Each reptile egg holds enough yolk to nourish the embryo until it hatches into a young one, so no larval feeding stage is needed.

questions.q:
Match each term with its meaning.
1. Larva
2. Yolk
3. External fertilisation
4. Internal fertilisation
a. Fusion of gametes inside the female's body
b. Nutritive substance stored in an egg
c. A feeding stage that hatches from the egg
d. Sperm released over eggs laid in water
questions.a: 1-c, 2-b, 3-d, 4-a: the larva is the feeding stage, yolk is stored food, external fertilisation happens in water and internal fertilisation inside the female.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Lizards generally produce more eggs at a time than frogs.
Reason (R): Fertilisation in lizards takes place inside the body of the female.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true: lizards lay about 2 to 20 eggs at a time, far fewer than the 5,000 to 50,000 of a frog, and their fertilisation is internal.

questions.q: True or False? In mammals, the zygote grows and develops inside the female's body. Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Mammals show internal fertilisation, and the zygote develops inside the mother; after birth the young are fed with breast milk.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: internal fertilisation, and the zygote develops inside the mother's body

questions.q: In the life cycle of a butterfly, (a) what is the feeding stage that hatches from the egg called, and (b) which stage comes between this feeding stage and the adult?
questions.a: (a) The larva. (b) The pupa.
s: (a) Larva
(b) Pupa

questions.q: A naturalist describes an animal that lives on land, has internal fertilisation and lays 3 eggs at a time, each with plenty of yolk. Predict, with a reason each: (i) whether the survival of its young is likely to be low or moderate to high, (ii) whether it hatches as a larva or as a young one, and (iii) which group it is most like among fish, frogs, lizards and birds.
questions.a: (i) Moderate to high: internal fertilisation protects the fertilised egg or embryo more, and few eggs go with better survival. (ii) A young one: the egg has enough yolk to nourish the embryo until it hatches, so no larval feeding stage is needed. (iii) Like lizards or birds: land animals with internal fertilisation that lay a few yolky eggs.
s: (i) Moderate to high survival, with the protection reason
(ii) Hatches as a young one, because the yolk is enough
(iii) Most like lizards or birds, with a reason

questions.q: Fish, frogs and insects lay several hundred to several thousand eggs at a time, each with only a little yolk. Answer in one step each: (i) What does yolk contain? (ii) Why can the mother not give each egg a large amount of yolk? (iii) How does the larva that hatches get its nutrition? (iv) What happens once the larva has gathered enough nutrition? Give one example.
questions.a: (i) Nutritive substances that nourish the developing embryo. (ii) She lays so many eggs that her body cannot provide large quantities of yolk for all of them. (iii) It feeds on organic wastes such as rotten food and manure. (iv) A transformation takes place and the adult body is formed, as in a butterfly or a frog.
s: (i) Nutritive substances for the embryo
(ii) Too many eggs for the mother to supply large yolk
(iii) Larva feeds on organic wastes
(iv) Transformation into the adult, with an example (butterfly or frog)

questions.q:
A farm school records three animals. A hen's egg develops for 21 days before hatching, and the chick pecks for its own food within hours. A pigeon's egg develops for about 18 days, and the young pigeon is fed by its parents for about four weeks after hatching. A goat kid develops inside its mother for about 150 days; it stands within hours of birth but drinks its mother's milk for about three months.
(a) Which of the three young ones can find its own food soon after hatching or birth?
(b) Compare the hen and the pigeon: how does the length of development inside the egg relate to the care needed after hatching?
(c) The goat kid develops longest, yet it still depends on its mother for food. Explain this using the chapter.
(d) A student concludes, 'The longer an embryo develops, the less care its young need, without any exception.' Evaluate this conclusion using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) The chick. (b) The chick develops longer (21 days) and needs no feeding after hatching, while the pigeon develops for a shorter time (about 18 days) and is fed for about four weeks, which fits the chapter's idea that the care needed broadly depends on how long the embryo develops. (c) The goat is a mammal, and mammals typically feed their young with breast milk for some time after birth. (d) Only partly supported: the hen and pigeon fit the broad trend, but the goat shows that a mammal still feeds its young on milk, so it is a broad tendency, not a rule without exceptions.
s: (a) The chick
(b) Longer development in the egg, less care after hatching (hen versus pigeon)
(c) Goat is a mammal; mammals feed young with breast milk after birth
(d) Conclusion is a broad trend only, with the goat as the exception

questions.q: Compare a frog and a lizard under five heads, using these facts: a frog lives in water and on land and lays 5,000 to 50,000 eggs at a time; a lizard lives on land and lays 2 to 20 eggs at a time. (i) Mode of fertilisation of each. (ii) How many times more eggs the frog lays than the lizard when each lays its smallest number. (iii) Likely survival of the young of each. (iv) Whether each passes through a larval stage, with a reason. (v) Why the large number of frog eggs does not mean that more frogs grow up.
questions.a: (i) Frog: external fertilisation; lizard: internal fertilisation. (ii) 5,000 / 2 = 2,500 times. (iii) Frog: low; lizard: moderate. (iv) Frog: yes, its egg has only enough yolk to make a larva (tadpole) that feeds and then transforms; lizard: no, a reptile egg has enough yolk to nourish the embryo until it hatches as a young one. (v) Frog eggs laid in water are destroyed by currents or eaten by other animals, so most are lost; the lizard's protected eggs survive better.
s: (i) Frog external, lizard internal
(ii) 2,500 times
(iii) Frog low, lizard moderate survival
(iv) Frog has a larval stage, lizard does not, with the yolk reason
(v) Frog eggs are lost to currents and other animals

questions.q: In the human male, in which organs are sperm produced?
questions.a: testes: the two oval organs, which lie in a pouch of skin called the scrotum.

questions.q: Which organ of the female reproductive system is a bag-like structure in which the foetus develops?
questions.a: uterus: it protects and nourishes the developing baby.

questions.q: In a typical 28-day cycle, an egg released on day 14 is not fertilised. Which sequence of events follows?
o: The egg degenerates in about a day; the lining breaks down around day 28 and leaves with blood
The egg waits in the oviduct until the next ovulation, and only then does the lining shed
The egg implants in the thick uterus lining, which then sheds 3 to 7 days later with blood
The egg and the thickened lining leave the body together on day 15, the day after ovulation
questions.a: The egg degenerates in about a day; the lining breaks down around day 28 and leaves with blood: the thickened lining is no longer needed, and its shedding is menstruation.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements comparing human gametes.
I. Sperm are produced in millions, while eggs are produced in few numbers.
II. Eggs are actively motile, while sperm are non-motile.
III. Sperm are larger than eggs.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I only. Statement II is the wrong way round (sperm are actively motile, eggs are non-motile), and statement III is wrong because sperm are very small and eggs are large.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In human males, the urethra is a common passage for urine and sperm.
Reason (R): The vas deferens, which carries sperm from the testes, opens into the urethra.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: sperm reach the urethra because the vas deferens opens into it.

questions.q: (a) What is gametogenesis? (b) Name the organs in which it takes place in a human male and in a human female.
questions.a: (a) Gametogenesis is the process of formation of gametes. (b) It takes place in the testes in males and in the ovaries in females.
s: (a) Formation of gametes
(b) Testes in males, ovaries in females

questions.q: A couple's first child is a girl. (a) Which sex chromosome did the mother pass on, and which did the father pass on? (b) For their next child, whose gamete will decide the sex, and what are the two possibilities?
questions.a: (a) Mother: X; father: X (the girl is XX). (b) The father's sperm decides: if it carries X the baby is a girl (XX); if it carries Y the baby is a boy (XY).
s: (a) Mother X, father X
(b) Father's sperm decides: X gives a girl (XX), Y gives a boy (XY)

questions.q: State (i) the typical length of the menstrual cycle, (ii) the age range at which it usually begins in girls, and (iii) the age around which it stops, with the name of that stage.
questions.a: (i) Every 21 to 35 days, often about 28 days. (ii) Between 10 and 14 years, at puberty. (iii) Around 50 years; this stage is menopause.
s: (i) 21 to 35 days (often about 28)
(ii) 10 to 14 years
(iii) Around 50 years, menopause

questions.q: Arun says, 'A woman releases only about one egg a month from puberty onwards, so her ovaries begin to hold eggs only when she reaches puberty.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. From puberty onwards, usually one mature egg is released every month from one of the ovaries (ovulation). But a girl's ovaries already hold millions of immature eggs at birth; puberty starts the monthly release of mature eggs, not the presence of eggs.
s: Agrees that one mature egg is usually released each month from puberty
States that the ovaries hold millions of immature eggs at birth
Verdict: partly right; puberty starts release, not the presence of eggs

questions.q: A school health club drafts a poster with five tips on hygiene during menstruation. Judge each tip as correct or wrong, and correct the wrong ones. (i) 'Wash the genital area with plenty of soap.' (ii) 'Change pads every 4 to 6 hours, or more often if the flow is heavy.' (iii) 'Flush used pads down the toilet.' (iv) 'A reusable pad may be used again while it is still slightly damp.' (v) 'Wash your hands with soap and water before and after changing a pad.'
questions.a: (i) Wrong: clean the genital area with water and avoid soap, which can disrupt the natural bacterial balance. (ii) Correct. (iii) Wrong: wrap used pads in newspaper or their wrapper and put them in a bin; do not flush them. (iv) Wrong: reusable pads must be completely dry before their next use. (v) Correct.
s: (i) Wrong; use water, avoid soap
(ii) Correct
(iii) Wrong; wrap and put in a bin
(iv) Wrong; must be completely dry
(v) Correct

questions.q: Table 11.5 says that sperm are very small, produced in millions, have no stored nutrients and are actively motile, while eggs are large, few, have stored nutrients and are non-motile. Each sperm has a head with genetic material and a long tail. Using these facts and the chapter, explain: (i) why the sperm needs its tail, (ii) why the body releases millions of sperm when only one fuses with the egg, (iii) which gamete's feature helps the zygote as it divides several times while travelling to the uterus before implanting, and (iv) why both gametes must carry 23 chromosomes.
questions.a: (i) The egg is non-motile and waits in the oviduct, so the sperm must swim through the reproductive tract to reach it; the tail lets it swim. (ii) Sperm must swim a long way and only some may reach the egg, so releasing millions makes it likely that one succeeds. (iii) The egg's stored nutrients: the zygote divides before it implants and receives nourishment from the uterus lining. (iv) Each gamete carries half of 46, so the zygote has 23 + 23 = 46, the same number as the parents.
s: (i) Tail lets the sperm swim to the non-motile egg
(ii) Only some sperm may reach the egg, so millions improve the chance
(iii) The egg's stored nutrients support the zygote before implantation
(iv) 23 + 23 = 46 keeps the parents' chromosome number

questions.q: Human pregnancy lasts about nine months. What are its three stages called?
questions.a: trimesters: the first, second and third trimester.

questions.q: Which of these is a barrier method of contraception?
questions.a: a vaginal cover: like a condom, it acts as a barrier that stops sperm from reaching the egg.

questions.q:
Match each stage of pregnancy with what happens in it.
1. First two months
2. From about the ninth week
3. Second trimester
4. Third trimester
a. The developing baby is called a foetus
b. The baby grows rapidly and gets ready for life outside the womb
c. The fertilised egg develops into an embryo and major organs start forming
d. The foetus grows bigger and stronger, and the mother can usually feel its movements
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-d, 4-b: embryo and organs in the first two months, foetus from about the ninth week, movements felt in the second trimester, rapid growth in the third.

questions.q: True or False? Some sexually transmitted infections cannot be cured yet. Give the verdict and state one way of preventing their spread.
questions.a: True. The chapter says some STIs are not curable yet; using condoms can prevent their transmission.
s: Verdict: True
Prevention: using condoms

questions.q: (a) Name any two sexually transmitted infections given in the chapter, other than HIV. (b) Which infection named in the chapter can eventually lead to AIDS?
questions.a: (a) Any two of gonorrhoea, herpes, syphilis and genital warts. (b) HIV.
s: (a) Any two of gonorrhoea, herpes, syphilis, genital warts
(b) HIV

questions.q: A health worker tells a village meeting, 'The surgical methods of contraception for men and for women work on the same basic idea.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Yes. In men the vas deferens is blocked, so sperm cannot travel out from the testes; in women the fallopian tubes are blocked, so the egg cannot travel along them. In both, the sperm and the egg cannot meet, so fertilisation cannot happen.
s: Men: the vas deferens is blocked
Women: the fallopian tubes are blocked
Verdict: Yes; in both the sperm and egg cannot meet

questions.q: Kavya is five months pregnant. Her weekly routine is: (i) she eats dal, eggs, leafy vegetables and fruit every day; (ii) she has skipped her last two check-ups because she feels well; (iii) she takes leftover painkiller tablets for headaches without asking anyone; (iv) she takes the short daily walk her doctor advised and rests in the afternoon; (v) she keeps her worries to herself because she does not want to trouble her family. Judge each habit as helpful or harmful for her and the baby, with a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (i) Helpful: a balanced diet rich in proteins, vitamins and minerals supports the baby's growth. (ii) Harmful: regular medical check-ups are needed even when she feels well. (iii) Harmful: she should not take any medicine without medical advice. (iv) Helpful: light exercise and rest as advised by the doctor. (v) Harmful: her emotional well-being matters, and support from family helps her stay healthy and stress-free.
s: (i) Helpful: balanced diet
(ii) Harmful: regular check-ups needed
(iii) Harmful: no medicine without medical advice
(iv) Helpful: light exercise and rest as advised
(v) Harmful: emotional well-being and family support matter

questions.q:
A school counsellor surveys 50 students of Class 9, aged 14 to 15. 42 of them say they have noticed the body changes of puberty, such as a growth spurt, a changing voice or the start of periods. Asked, 'Do you feel able to handle strong feelings and make thoughtful decisions on your own?', 18 students say yes.
(a) What percentage of the students report body changes?
(b) What percentage of all the students feel able to handle their feelings and decisions?
(c) Using the chapter, explain why the two percentages differ.
(d) A parent at the meeting says, 'Since most of them are physically mature, they are ready for adult responsibilities.' Evaluate this view using your answers to (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) 42 / 50 x 100 = 84%. (b) 18 / 50 x 100 = 36%. (c) Sexual maturity, such as sperm production in boys and menstrual cycles in girls, comes gradually with body growth, but emotional maturity, which means handling feelings, communicating clearly and making thoughtful decisions, takes longer. (d) The view is not supported: 84% show physical changes but only 36% feel emotionally ready; a body becoming capable of reproduction does not mean a person is ready for adult responsibilities.
s: (c) Sexual maturity comes gradually; emotional maturity takes longer, with its meaning
(d) View not supported: physical maturity is not readiness, using 84% versus 36%

questions.q:
Ananya's pregnancy is being followed at a government hospital. Take her pregnancy as about 39 weeks, divided into three trimesters of about 13 weeks each. She has check-ups in week 8, week 20 and week 30, and a final visit in week 38. At the final visit, the doctor says that a normal vaginal birth may not be safe for her.
(a) At the week-8 check-up, is the developing baby an embryo or a foetus? Give a reason.
(b) In which trimester is the week-20 check-up, and what can Ananya usually feel by then?
(c) In which trimester is the week-30 check-up, and what is happening to the baby during it?
(d) What normally pushes the baby out during childbirth, and what can the doctors do in Ananya's case?
questions.a: (a) An embryo: it is called a foetus only from about the ninth week. (b) The second trimester (weeks 14 to 26); she can usually feel the foetus move. (c) The third trimester (weeks 27 to 39); the baby grows rapidly and gets ready for life outside the womb. (d) Strong contractions of the muscles of the uterus push the foetus out through the birth canal; since a normal birth may not be safe, doctors may use medical or surgical procedures to deliver the baby safely.
s: (a) Embryo, because it becomes a foetus only from about week 9
(b) Second trimester; mother feels the foetus move
(c) Third trimester; rapid growth and readiness for life outside
(d) Uterine muscle contractions; doctors may use medical or surgical procedures
